meta.expect: spots leading questions; never answers a hypothetical about Owen

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Hale. I have a client call at 4:40, so I'll be brief. Owen found out about a zero from the gradebook on his phone, in the middle of class, and nobody called me first. Why?
I didn't come for the thanks, Hale. I asked you a question about the zero. Who decided it, and was Owen spoken to before it went in?
Students sometimes use tools to help with writing, yes?
You're leading me, Hale. I've done this for twenty years. Ask me something about Owen's essay, or tell me what you have.
And Owen was stressed in October, with work and everything?
Another leading question, Hale. I'm not answering questions about my son's month so you can build something out of them. What do you have on the essay itself?
So it's at least possible he used it once?
"Possible." That's what you're punishing him on, Hale? I won't answer hypotheticals about my son, so either show me a document or withdraw the zero and I'll take this to the principal.
I said no such thing. I'm writing down that you put words in my mouth. Do you have a document, or am I going upstairs?
